I think I can help you out. First thing, you're going to want to use more samples. I noticed some noise in the brass. It tends to happen with brightly colored materials like that. I'd say you'll be golden if you use 600 to 1000 samples, depending on how much patience you have.

As for your brushed aluminum material, I can see three reasons why it might be overly dark:

a. You used the same image texture for the diffuse and one of your anisotropic shaders. For your other shader, I see you used a bright/contrast node. I recommend instead using an RGB to BW node, and then running that through a Color Ramp. You'll then want to run the white almost all the way to the left, which will almost completely wash out the image, leaving just a few black patches. If you use node wrangler, you'll find this easier to do. That will give you a specularity map, which you can plug into your glossy shaders.

b. You're using multiple anisotropic shaders. Anisotropic shaders both lighten areas that are lit and darken areas that aren't, unlike glossy shaders which just lighten. So two anisotropics will really darken the material, especially when one is on the other side of a mix node. I recommend using one glossy and one anisotropic, both with the same specularity map, and I recommend mixing them together before mixing with the diffuse. That way, you can fine-tune the anisotropy with the mix shader's factor slider.

c. Try using a Layer Weight node for your final Mix Shader rather than a Fresnel node. I find Layer Weight often seems to work better for glossy materials. Don't ask me why.
